food.text: In the 19th century, Iranians shifted from eating opium to smoking it, which created a surge in addiction far more severe than before. Opium smoking became a social plague, and the profitability of the crop led farmers to turn farmland over to it, disrupting food production. According to reviewer James McHugh, the surge in addiction contributed to the 1870 famine, and Iran became a major opium exporter.
food.source_title: The Pursuit of Pleasure: Drugs and Stimulants in Iranian History, 1500–1900

food.text: The Qajars projected greater piety and temperance, because their legitimacy was weaker and they depended on clerical support. Even so, wine drinking continued in private, and it increasingly included imported spirits like vodka and champagne.

food.text: The Persian famine of 1870–1872 was a period of mass starvation and disease in Iran (Persia) during the Qajar era. It is the best documented famine in Iranian history and affected almost the whole country. Some cities, including Shahrud, Kerman, and Birjand, managed to avoid the catastrophe.

In March 1890, Naser al-Din Shah gave Major G. F. Talbot a fifty-year monopoly over the production, sale and export of Iranian tobacco. Iranians grew a variety of tobacco that was much prized in foreign markets and not grown elsewhere, which made the crop especially valuable.
The New York Herald blamed the famine of 1870–1872 on a rise in the price of cotton. It said Persian farmers abandoned grain farming and planted cotton as a cash crop instead.

Under the tobacco monopoly, called the Régie, all producers and owners of tobacco had to sell to its agents. The agents resold the tobacco at a price agreed between the company and the sellers, with disputes settled by compulsory arbitration. Talbot paid the shah £15,000 a year plus a quarter of the yearly profits.

In Qajar times, Isfahan, Yazd, Shiraz, Kashan, Hamadan and Rasht were the principal manufacturing centers, and some of them produced wine and other alcoholic drinks. These included araq, a distilled spirit, and buza, a fermented drink made from barley or millet.

Shoko Okazaki argued that two consecutive years of severe drought were the main cause of the 1870–1872 famine, and rejected the idea that growing more opium and cotton played a part. He blamed its effects on senior bureaucrats, landlords, grain dealers and high-ranking religious officials who hoarded grain and manipulated the market.

Scholars do not agree on how many people died in the famine of 1870–1872, though it is believed to have caused a considerable decline in Iran's population. Contemporary observers gave figures from 0.2–0.3 million deaths (Frederic John Goldsmid) to 3 million (James Bassett), with others giving 1.5 million and 2.5 million, while Fereydun Adamiyat calculates around 2 million. Gad G. Gilbar's 1.5 million could be between 15% and 20–25% of the population, and one calculation puts Iran's population at 10 million in 1850 and 6 million in 1873.

In December 1891, Grand Ayatollah Mirza Shirazi issued a widely obeyed fatwa against tobacco use. Merchants in Tehran, Shiraz, Mashhad and Isfahan joined the protest, and by January 1892 the shah had canceled the concession.

Reviewer Willem Floor noted that Rudolph Matthee's book has much quantified commercial data on coffee but very little on tea. That is a striking gap, given that the book describes tea as gradually displacing coffee as Iran's national beverage.
food.source_title: The Pursuit of Pleasure: Drugs and Stimulants in Iranian History, 1500–1900

food.text: Dry white Shiraz wines were fermented with significant stem contact, which should have made them rich in tannins. The sweet ones were not made this way.

art.text: Qajaresque Neo-Baroque architecture was an extravagant, eclectic style of 19th-century Persia that blended traditional Persian art with the theatrical luxury of Baroque Revival design. It flourished particularly under Naser al-Din Shah Qajar and is famous for its extreme use of stucco.

Photography became popular in Iran during the late Qajar era, and Naser al-Din Shah embraced it enthusiastically. From 1858 he photographed the residents of his harem, and the art historian Pamela Karimi notes that some of the women were shown unveiled and "in erotic poses". His own mother, Malek Jahan Khanum, was the first Iranian woman to be photographed, and he ignored the cultural and religious limits on depicting women. During his rule, painting and photography influenced each other in both style and composition.

Fath-Ali Shah at the Hunt is an oil on canvas painting with lavish gilding by the Iranian artist Mihr 'Ali, created around 1810. It shows the shah on a white horse, racing wildly through a lush plain, his horse seeming to soar with all four legs in midair and his beard blowing to the left as he charges. He deftly pierces a ferocious lion with a glittering spear, while twenty-two of his sons, each marked by a crown, are arranged in an elliptical pattern around him.

Mirza Baba and Mihr 'Ali were the most prominent painters of the first two decades of 19th-century Iran. Mirza Baba came from an Imami family of Isfahan and worked at the court in Tehran under Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar and Fath-Ali Shah Qajar.

Qajaresque interiors reversed traditional Iranian residential layouts, moving from inward-looking private spaces to outward-looking public displays. Reception halls called talar were re-engineered around grand, double-flight imperial staircases. High, flat-framed ceilings replaced mud-brick vaults, letting light stream through large street-facing windows and deep balconies.

Kamal-ol-molk (1845 to 1940) came from a family of court painters but also trained with a painter who had studied in Europe. After a career at court, he visited Europe in 1898 at the age of 47 and stayed for some four years. He was one of the artists who introduced a more European style to Persian painting.

Qajar-era wall and ceiling decoration shifted from abstract patterns to Western-style figurative realism and oil painting techniques. Interior tilework abandoned Safavid geometric designs for pictures of European landscapes, flowers, cherubs and human figures. Some figures were concubines of the Qajar harem, dressed in contemporary Victorian attire.

Traditional Iranian mirror work, called Ayeneh-kari, changed radically in this period. Safavid and early Islamic mirror work used tiny diamond-cut geometric shapes arranged in mathematical patterns. Inspired by the mirror halls Naser al-Din Shah Qajar saw on his European tours, late 19th-century craftsmen switched to massive unbroken panels of imported Venetian sheet glass.

Fath-Ali Shah at the Hunt was presented as a royal gift to the British and possibly arrived in England with ambassador Gore Ouseley in 1814. It now hangs on the ceiling of the Ashok Hall in the Rashtrapati Bhavan in New Delhi, having been transferred from London to British India in 1929.

In 1858 the Qajar court appointed the French photographer Frances Carhlian to teach photography, spreading the collodion method in the state. He was the first male foreign photographer to depict Iranian women. Later, Dust Mohammed Khan Mo'ayyer-ol-Mamalek and his brother Mirza set up a photo studio in their house.

Gertrude Bell traveled through Iran in 1911, motivated by archaeological research. She concentrated on photographing Iranian landscapes and nature sites rather than women. Among all her photographs there is only one woman, shown as part of a family portrait.

Carpet weaving suffered from the introduction of synthetic dyes during the second half of the nineteenth century. The art has gone through periods of decline during political unrest or under the pressure of commercial demands. Modern production has revived traditional natural dyes and tribal patterns.

war.text: In 1804 the Russians invaded and sacked the Iranian town of Ganja, massacring and expelling thousands of its inhabitants. This began the Russo-Persian War of 1804 to 1813. The Qajar army suffered a major defeat, and Iran was forced to cede most of its Caucasian territories.

The Anglo-Persian War arose when Britain opposed an attempt by Iran to press its claim on Herat, which Iran had conquered in 1856. British forces under Major General Sir James Outram fought in two theatres, near Bushehr and in southern Mesopotamia. Iran withdrew from Herat in 1857 and signed the treaty of Paris.

Under the Treaty of Gulistan in 1813, Iran ceded most of its Caucasian territories, comprising modern-day Georgia, Dagestan, and most of Azerbaijan. The treaty ended the Persian defeat in the war that began with the sack of Ganja in 1804.

The Russian Empire backed Persian sieges of Herat in 1837 to 1838 and 1856 as part of the Great Game. For Persia, the expansion into Afghanistan was an attempt to compensate for the territories lost to Russia in the Caucasus.

Persia declared neutrality in the First World War, but Russia already had forces there. The Persian Cossack Brigade had eight squadrons, a small infantry battalion and a horse battery of six Krupp guns, with a total strength not exceeding 2,000. Russia had occupied Tabriz in 1909, and Urmia and Khoi in 1910.

Abbas Mirza, inspired by the Europeans, abolished the use of the zamburak on the battlefield. He instead used heavier artillery pulled by horses or mules, similar to Europe. The zamburak's musical and artillery branches were preserved only for ceremonial purposes.

In the Fourth Russo-Persian War, 20,000 Persian men captured the fortress of Lankaran in the Talesh province on 12 August 1812. In October 1812 the Russians defeated them at Aslanduz in the Ardabil province, destroying the Persian artillery and forcing a retreat to Tauris. The Persians were defeated again at Lankaran on 13 January 1813. Earlier in the war, Ganja had been occupied and sacked, and 3,000 of its citizens were killed.

Russian forces kept up the pressure on Persian troops in the middle years of the Russo-Persian War. They captured Karakapet in 1806 and Karababa in 1808, occupied Ganja in 1809, and took Akhalkalaki in 1810. Ganja had earlier been occupied and sacked, with 3,000 citizens killed.

The British advanced inland and defeated the Iranian field army at Koosh-Ab on 8 February 1857. The 1st Qashqai Regiment formed an infantry square with kneeling ranks and fired volleys at the charging 3rd Bombay Light Cavalry. In the close fighting its standard-bearer was shot and the standard was taken. Moore's horse was shot and bayoneted and fell on its rider. The Poona Horse still carries the captured Standard, surmounted by a silver hand and bearing a Persian inscription.

The Iranian infantry to the right of the left flank began fleeing in disorder at the Battle of Khoshab, and as the line wavered the Poona Horse spiked the two guns on the Iranian left. The British record gave one officer and 18 men killed and four officers and 60 wounded, though other records give 220 killed and 64 wounded. The British claimed about 700 Iranian casualties, while the Iranian government claimed 1,000 British killed and wounded. After the retreat, Tehran relieved Shoja ol-Molk of command by 14 February. Mirza Mohammad Khan Qajar-Dolu, Commandant of the Shah's Bodyguard, took over and later became generalissimo (Sepahsalar) and Iran's first minister of war.

After the Battle of Khoshab, the British army feared raids and ambushes by Tangestani guerilla fighters, so Outram avoided the road from Chahkootah and took the coastal passage via Shif. Even so, the guerilla fighters of Ziarat ambushed them. The march back was made in torrential rain, with mud deep enough to pull a man's boots from his feet. The troops had covered 46 miles in 41 hours to meet the enemy, a further 20 miles overnight after the battle, and another 24 miles to Bushire after six hours of rest. Pitiless rains and winds formed a swamp with knee-deep water around the battalions.

literature.text: In the 19th century, Persian literature entered a new era. The change was exemplified at the court of Nasereddin Shah, when the reform-minded prime minister Amir Kabir chastised the poet Habibollah Qa'ani Shirazi for 'lying' in a panegyric qasida written in Kabir's honor.

The Constitutional Revolution of 1905-1911 contributed to the expansion of literary expression in Persian. It also brought the emergence of new forms of political and social criticism, as writers increasingly experimented with new forms and genres.

The introduction and translation of European plays in nineteenth-century Iran contributed to the emergence of modern Iranian theatre. Playwrights including Mirza Fatali Akhundov contributed through works that circulated in Persian.

In 1859, the works of Voltaire were first translated into Persian by Jalal al-Din Mirza Qajar, a freethinking prince. He had studied in France on behalf of Amir Kabir in 1843 and presented a manuscript to Naser al-Din Shah. Voltaire's books then became available to the educated class.

Amir Kabir saw the poetry that had developed during the Qajar period as detrimental to 'progress' and 'modernization'. Similar concerns were voiced by Fath-'Ali Akhundzadeh, Mirza Aqa Khan Kermani, and Mirza Malkom Khan, who also called for change in Persian poetry in literary terms, always linking it to social concerns.

Neshat (1759-1829) became a major figure of the bazgasht-e adabi, or 'literary return', movement at the Qajar court. He was an avid supporter of Fath-Ali Shah's promotion of such poets, and is regarded as one of the foremost poets and stylists of Persian of the early Qajar era.

Neshat's poetry was compiled into a book called Ganjineh-ye Neshat, or 'Treasure of Joy', published in Tehran in 1850 after his death. In 1864-1865, Naser al-Din Shah Qajar had all of his literary works compiled and lithographed into one volume with five sections.
Neshat's prose included didactic pieces and short anecdotes, written in imitation of Saadi Shirazi's Golestan. The style was described as a very refined prose interspersed with poetry.

Writers and journalists such as Mirza Jahangir Khan Shirazi and Farrokhi Yazdi became prominent voices of the constitutionalist movement. They joined its calls for political reform, freedom and social change during the Constitutional Revolution of 1905-1911.

Balochi, spoken by the Baloch people throughout Balochistan, has a literary tradition that starts from the early 19th century. It is one of the modern Iranian literatures alongside Persian, Ossetian, Kurdish and Pashto.
Gurani was once used as a court language by the Qajar-era Kurdish vassaldom of Ardalan. Its literary tradition includes the works of the 19th-century poet and historian Mastura Ardalan of Senna.

The 19th-century novelist Raffi was among the Iranian Armenians who contributed to Armenian literature. Schools dedicated especially to Armenian communities were established since the 19th century in Azerbaijan, Isfahan, and Tehran, encouraging Armenian writing throughout modern Iran.

Much of Neshat's writing consists of official papers and letters. One especially noteworthy letter went to George III, in which Neshat expressed grief about the breakdown of amicable relations between Great Britain and Iran.

Near the end of the 19th century, a Persian newspaper called Miftah al-Zafar (1897) campaigned for the formation of Anjuman-i Ma'arif. This was an academy devoted to strengthening the Persian language as a scientific language.

science.text: Modern science in Iran accelerated in the nineteenth century. Two developments drove it: the founding of the institution called Darolfonoon in 1851 and the dispatch of Iranian students to Europe. Together they brought modern scientific education and European scientific knowledge into the country.
Modern academic medicine began in Iran in 1878, when Joseph Cochran established a medical college in Urmia. He is often credited with founding Iran's first contemporary medical college.
In 1900 the first telephone patent was assigned to Basir-ol-mamalek. From then on, telephone services began working in Tehran, bringing a new communication technology to the Iranian capital.
science.source_title: Ministry of Information and Communications Technology of Iran

science.text: Urmia University credits Joseph Cochran with lowering the infant mortality rate in the region. He is also credited with founding Westminster Hospital in Urmia, one of Iran's first modern hospitals.

In 1882 a lithographed booklet called the Tariff of the Great Post Office of Iran was published. It displayed maps of telegram offices, post offices, pony post roads and the postal network. It described Iran as having seven main and five secondary postal lines.
science.source_title: Ministry of Information and Communications Technology of Iran

science.text: Adolf Fonahn's Zur Quellenkunde der Persischen Medizin, published in Leipzig in 1910, counted over 400 works on medicine in the Persian language. This count excluded authors such as Avicenna, who wrote in Arabic.

politics.text: Qajar Iran was the Iranian state ruled by the Qajar dynasty from 1789 to 1925. Its founder, Agha Mohammad Khan, was known as one of the cruelest kings even by 18th-century Iranian standards: he razed cities, massacred entire populations, and blinded some 20,000 men in Kerman for defending it against his siege. He defeated all rivals from the Zand and Afsharid dynasties, was formally crowned Shah in 1796, and was assassinated in 1797. His nephew Fath-Ali Shah succeeded him.

In the first decades of the 19th century, Qajar Iran lost much of its conquered Caucasus territory to the Russian Empire. The losses covered modern-day eastern Georgia, Dagestan, Azerbaijan and Armenia. Iran also faced major challenges to its sovereignty from the Russian and British empires in the Great Game.

The Guarded Domains of Iran was the official name of Iran from the Safavid era until the early 20th century. The name alluded to the country's decentralised administration and its cultural and ethnic diversity. Territorial losses under the Qajars in the 19th century led to a new understanding of what the name meant.

Concessions to foreign powers eroded Iran's sovereignty and became a focal point of nationalist resistance. This showed most notably in the Tobacco Protest of 1891 to 1892 and the Persian Constitutional Revolution of 1905 to 1911.

Iran's ancient cultural relationship with the Caucasus lasted until the 19th century. Following the Russo-Persian Wars, Iran lost Azerbaijan, Armenia, eastern Georgia and parts of the North Caucasus to Imperial Russia.
In the Tobacco Revolt of 1891, Iranians boycotted tobacco to protest a British monopoly concession. The revolt showed how everyday substances could catalyze political resistance.
politics.source_title: The Pursuit of Pleasure: Drugs and Stimulants in Iranian History, 1500–1900

politics.text: Agha Mohammad Shah was assassinated in Shusha in 1797 while preparing a second expedition against Georgia. His first campaign had ended with the fall of Tbilisi: the Georgians, hopelessly outnumbered, were defeated, and the Iranian army marched back laden with spoil and carrying off many thousands of captives. In 1799 the Russians marched into Tbilisi, and the weakened and devastated Georgian kingdom, its capital half in ruins, was easily absorbed by Russia in 1801.

Iran could not accept the cession of Transcaucasia and Dagestan, which had formed part of the concept of Iran for centuries. This led to the Russo-Persian War of 1804 to 1813, which began when the Russians invaded and sacked the Iranian town of Ganja, massacring and expelling thousands of its inhabitants, and to the war of 1826 to 1828. Both ended in forced cessions to Russia under the treaties of Gulistan in 1813 and Turkmenchay in 1828.

The Persian Constitutional Revolution was driven by intellectuals and merchants who demanded an end to Qajar corruption and foreign domination. The 1906 Constitution established the Majlis, or parliament. In 1908 the Majlis tried to annul the D'Arcy oil concession but was suppressed by Mohammad Ali Shah.
Before 1876, Iran's postal affairs were handled by a bureau. Naser-aldin Shah then ordered that it be converted into a full ministry, and Amin-almolk was selected to carry out its operations.
politics.source_title: Ministry of Information and Communications Technology of Iran

politics.text: Under British pressure, Mohammad Shah Qajar issued a firman suppressing the slave trade in 1848. Slavery itself was not abolished in Iran until 1929.

Iranian intellectuals gathered in secret societies, such as Mirza Malkam Khan's Faramosh Khaneh, which was based on Masonic lodges. They spread their ideas by distributing leaflets and newspapers. They stressed reform of the land and administrative system and limiting rulers within the framework of the law.

The 1891 tobacco boycott did not end the monopoly. According to reviewer Willem Floor, the regime was imposed anyway in 1892 through a nominally Ottoman company, which resulted in worse financial consequences for the peasants.
politics.source_title: The Pursuit of Pleasure: Drugs and Stimulants in Iranian History, 1500–1900

politics.text: After being defeated by Britain, Iran signed the Treaty of Paris in 1857, in which it agreed to relinquish all territorial claims to Herat or any other area within Afghanistan.

The Persian Constitutional Revolution of 1905 to 1911 established the first Iranian parliament and introduced a constitution limiting the powers of the monarchy. Continued British and Russian opposition to the constitutional movement kept Iran unstable.

In 1906 the postal ministry was restructured, and the telegraph bureau was put under its administration. The result was the Ministry of Post and Telegraph, which joined two communication technologies in one Iranian ministry.
politics.source_title: Ministry of Information and Communications Technology of Iran

politics.text: Mostashar al-Dowleh's thoughts were incompatible with the temperament of Naser al-Din Shah, so he suffered the same fate that befell all libertarians at that time. The Shah had him chained and imprisoned in the Rokniyeh mansion in 1891. He was kept alone in prison, not allowed to meet anyone, not even other prisoners in Qazvin. He was tortured in prison and died a few years later, in 1895.

Abol-Qasem Qa'em-Maqam experimented with words that rhymed with mahrus to create prose resembling a political slogan that encouraged the defence of Iran. Russia (Rus) was seen as an ominous (manhus) threat, endangering the Qajars' territorial integrity and their honor (namus). The loss of the Caucasian provinces in the two wars with Russia damaged the Qajars' reputation as guardians of Iran.

Prince Majd ed-Dowleh Amirsoleimani was one of Iran's most influential politicians of his time. He was a key court figure through the reigns of several Qajar Shahs, including Nasser al-Din Shah, Mozaffar ad-Din Shah and Mohammad Ali Shah.

Amin-almolk served as Minister of Tasks and Council and also ran the postal ministry. In 1877, after a year as its minister, he resigned from the Ministry of Tasks and Council to devote more time to it. During the 19th century Mirza Rahim served as his deputy.
politics.source_title: Ministry of Information and Communications Technology of Iran

philosophy.text: The Iranian Enlightenment brought new ideas into traditional Iranian society from the mid-19th to the early 20th centuries. After Iran's defeat in the last Russo-Persian War (1826–1828), cultural exchanges led to new ideas among the educated class.

Dar al-Fonun was the first modern university in Iran, and the arrival of foreign professors caused the thoughts of European thinkers to enter the country. It was followed by the first signs of enlightenment and intellectual movements in Iran.

Intellectual life in 19th-century Iran spread through education, translations, the press, travel, and new institutions such as Dar al-Funun. These debates fed into the Constitutional Revolution and later arguments over nationalism, Islam, democracy, and modernity.

Iran's defeat in the war of 1826–1828 with Russia made the military, scientific and economic backwardness of the country clear to the educated class. As a result, a number of French-speaking princes, students, and literates traveled to France in 1843 to study.

Intellectual groups in this period formed secret societies, including Mirza Malkam Khan's Faramosh Khaneh, which was based on Masonic lodges. They spread their ideas through leaflets and newspapers, and stressed land and administrative reform, a smaller role for the clergy, and limits on rulers within the law.
The Constitutional Revolution of 1905–1911 drew on ideas of liberalism, representative government, social justice and civil rights. It led to the establishment of the National Consultative Assembly.

Iranian intellectuals of the nineteenth century differed over which reforms were needed. Some stressed constitutional government and the rule of law, while others stressed modern education and science. Their debates were carried through education, translations, the press, travel and institutions such as Dar al-Funun.

Many intellectual customs in Qajar Iran were inspired by the French, including the tradition of setting up salons. Secret societies were mostly formed in the homes of wealthy princes interested in science.

Jalal al-Din Mirza presented a manuscript of his Voltaire translation to Naser al-Din Shah. After a while, Voltaire's books became available to the educated class, and translating Western philosophers, above all Voltaire, was a significant factor in the growth of the Iranian intellectual movement.

Mostashar al-Dowleh's thoughts were incompatible with the temperament of Naser al-Din Shah, so he suffered the same fate that befell all libertarians at that time. He was chained and imprisoned in the Rokniyeh mansion in 1891 by the Shah, alone in prison and not allowed to meet anyone, not even other prisoners in Qazvin. He was tortured in prison and died a few years later, in 1895.

culture.text: After Iran's defeat in the last Russo-Persian War (1826–1828), cultural exchanges led to new ideas among the educated class. The establishment of Dar al-Fonun, the first modern university in Iran, and the arrival of foreign professors brought the thoughts of European thinkers into the country.

During Qajar rule, many wealthy households imported Black African women and children as slaves to do their domestic work. They were enslaved alongside Circassian slaves. Most were drawn from the Zanj, Bantu-speaking peoples of Southeast Africa, in an area roughly covering modern Tanzania, Mozambique and Malawi.

Westerners commonly called the country Persia, and for international purposes Persia was the norm. Yet the Harmsworth Encyclopaedia, circa 1907, noted under its entry for Iran that the name was now the official designation of Persia. This shows an internal preference for Iran already existed.

After the war of 1826–1828 with Russia, a number of French-speaking princes, students and literates traveled to France in 1843 to study. They included Mirza Malkam Khan. Many intellectual customs in Qajar Iran, including the tradition of setting up salons, were inspired by the French.

After the Russo-Persian wars of 1804 to 1813 and 1826 to 1828, large migrations of so-called Caucasian Muhajirs set off for mainland Iran. Some of these groups included the Ayrums, Qarapapaqs, Circassians and Shia Lezgins. According to The Cambridge History of Iran, the steady encroachment of Russian troops, General Yermolov's brutal punitive expeditions and misgovernment drove large numbers of Muslims, and even some Georgian Christians, into exile in Iran. Later, from 1864, another mass expulsion of Caucasian Muslims followed the Russian victory in the Caucasian War.

In 1892, Indian merchants funded the Bandar Abbas Vishnu Temple, built by the Arya Samaj. It is now used as the Anthropology Museum of the Persian Gulf. Wall paintings and statues of Hindu deities, such as Lord Krishna, are still visible inside.
